The dataset and the annotation guidelines are designed to uncover sen- timent expressed by an obfuscated language. 3.1 Annotation Guidelines We annotate aspect and sentiment for each para- graph from selected sections in the document. We specify 16 aspects to cover most topics discussed in the financial reports that might be useful for predicting certain financial behavior in the capital market (Table 1). The sentiment labels are nega- tive, positive, and neutral. Each paragraph might be annotated with multiple aspect-sentiment pairs. While aspect annotation is fairly straightforward, sentiment expressed in official financial reports show unique characteristics that cannot be ade- quately captured using typical sentiment annotation guidelines. For this reason, we call this annotation obfuscated sentiment. General sentiment analysis often fails to reflect investor emotions accurately because many seemingly positive statements in re- ports are crafted to mitigate underlying negative implications for readers. This phenomenon is illus- trated in Figures 1 and 2. Figure 1 outlines how the company faced finan- cial difficulties due to political instability and re- sponded by expanding into new advertising media. Although this expansion is framed as an optimistic strategy, it may also suggest that the company is struggling and reacting to economic pressures. In- vestors might perceive this move as a sign of fi- nancial instability, raising concerns about the com- pany’s overall performance and prospects. Taken from the paragraph located in the differ- ent section of another company, Figure 2 discusses the company’s investment in renewable energy, pre- senting it as a positive strategic move supported by stable cash flow and government policy. How- ever, it also acknowledges economic challenges like stagflation, which could impact the investment. The conditional future expansion based on funds and returns suggests uncertainty. This focus on positives might obscure underlying risks and raise concerns about the company’s ability to manage these challenges effectively. The examples above illustrate that language used in official financial report often use optimistic language to frame the company’s strategies positively while subtly redi- recting attention from underlying risks and chal- lenges. Therefore, the creation of a financial senti- ment dataset requires careful attention to develop new sentiment guidelines. 3.2 Data Annotation and Statistics All annotations were conducted by four annotators with backgrounds in economics, ensuring that the interpretations of financial language were grounded in domain expertise. Before beginning large-scale annotation, the annotators underwent a training phase in which they practiced on sample para- graphs and iteratively refined their understanding of the guidelines. This training ensured that all annotators applied the aspect and sentiment criteria consistently. The average inter-annotator Cohen’s kappa score reached 0.73 for aspect annotation and 0.77 for sentiment annotation, both falling within the substantial agreement range (Landis and Koch, 1977). These results demonstrate that, despite the challenges posed by obfuscated and strategically framed corporate language, the annotation guide- lines successfully enabled reliable and consistent labeling across all annotators. The performance of WangchanBERTa suggests that sen- timent classification benefits from considering sen- tence context, along with keywords (Table 5). The WangchanBERTa model achieves a high 79% ac- curacy, outperforming models relying solely on keywords like Maximum Entropy (74%). This indicates the importance of paragraph-level con- text for efficient sentiment analysis. Adding con- text beyond keywords improves accuracy by 5%. Despite having to operate 16-way classification, both BERT-based models show good effectiveness in real-world data aggregation. The CNN model, which tests the efficiency of using very narrow con- textual information, does not perform better than models using keywords for aspect classification. This suggests that expanding the contextual consid- eration to at least the sentence level is necessary to achieve higher accuracy in aspect classification. WangchanBERTa achieves a good 77% accuracy, which is considered high compared to similar Thai language datasets (Table 5). This suggests that the text from Form 56-1 may have common pat- terns across companies. The most efficient model is WangchanBERTa, followed by CNN and Max- imum Entropy, respectively. CNN, which utilizes local context, performs better than Maximum En- tropy in extracting signals for sentiment classifi- cation. This illustrates that using keywords alone is insufficient for sentiment analysis, emphasizing the need for broader context. WangchanBERTa can consider a broader linguistic context than CNN due to its use of self-attention, which can analyze dependencies between distant constituents of a sen- tence. Therefore, WangchanBERTa is the most suitable model for this task. 6 Event Study We want to study the effects of financial reports on their respective companies’ stock prices. The study of impacts of a particular event on firm’s stock is called ’event study’ (MacKinlay, 1997). This study relies on the assumption that capital market reflects the information about the firm in company’s stock price. To quantify an event’s economic impact, abnormal returns are calculated by deducting the normal returns, which would have been realized if the analyzed event has not occurred, from the actual return. We had tried estimating the normal returns from three expected return models: (1) constant mean model using the average return of the stock over the past year, (2) market model utilizing linear regression modeling of the SET market index to calculate returns over the past year,

Finally, the abnormal return deducted from the output of 6 Fama-French model was selected to be used in re- gression analysis in the next section, since there was no significant difference observed when com- paring the results of each model. In this context, the analyzed event is designed to be one day after the submitted date of Form 56-1 via SETLink, a portal for document submission to The Stock Exchange of Thailand, by companies. According to SET regulations, financial reports are published the day after their submission. Our study focuses on 189 non-financial companies listed in the SET Index or MAI Index, spanning returns from 2015 to 2022. The methodology involves three sets of event windows: ±5 days, ±3 days, and ±1 day, with an estimation size of 250 days. 6.1 Regression Analysis To investigate the impact of sentiment extracted from Thai financial reports on the Thai stock mar- kets, a linear regression model was utilized. The model aimed to confirm the correlation between sentiment expressed in various aspects, treated as predictors, and cumulative average abnormal re- turn (CAAR), the dependent variable. The dataset encompasses 700 observations pertaining to 189 firms listed on the Stock Exchange of Thailand (SET) for the period 2015 to 2022. Regarding the sentiment, we extract sentiments and aspects from the financial reports of those companies by utiliz- ing the optimal language models from previous sections. The automatic annotation of aspect-based sentiment was done by the fine-tuned Wangchan- BERTa model. We structure this experiment as a cross-sectional analysis based on the industries in which compa- nies are registered to mitigate overlapping event windows across companies, which could possibly lead to clustering problem in statistical analysis. The event windows are calculated with the refer- enced event date as the release date of the document plus one day (t+1). The regression models incorpo- rate five firm-level control variables to account for financial and operational characteristics that may influence the dependent variable. The variables are defined as follows: • Firm size: measured as the natural logarithm of the firm’s market capitalization. • Tobin’s Q: calculated as the natural logarithm of the ratio of market capitalization to total assets. • Return on assets (ROA): the ratio of net in- come to total assets. • Leverage: the ratio of total liabilities to total assets. • Volatility: the standard deviation of firm re- turns, estimated from the 12 months preceding the event date. For each observation, sentiment is represented using either one-hot embedding or sentiment score. The main regression predictors are derived from the textual analysis of financial documents. Each variable is defined below: • Aspect: a categorical variable representing the type

re- turns, estimated from the 12 months preceding the event date. For each observation, sentiment is represented using either one-hot embedding or sentiment score. The main regression predictors are derived from the textual analysis of financial documents. Each variable is defined below: • Aspect: a categorical variable representing the type of information in each sentence, with 16 possible types as described earlier. • Sentiment: a categorical variable indicating emotional polarity with three classes: nega- tive, neutral, and positive. • Source: the section of the financial docu- ment from which a sentence is extracted; three sources are used: Management Discussion & Analysis (MDA), Sustainability, and Risk. • Industry: a set of dummy variables repre- senting the firm’s industry classification, with eight broad industry categories defined by the Stock Exchange of Thailand (SET). • Score adapted from Tan et al. Our regression analysis reveals a nuanced relationship between sentiment expressed in Form 56-1 reports and subsequent mar- ket reactions. When using only aggregated senti- ment categories (Model 1), none of the coefficients reach statistical significance, suggesting that simple polarity labels (positive/neutral/negative) alone are insufficient to

language affect Thai stock market? Our regression analysis reveals a nuanced relationship between sentiment expressed in Form 56-1 reports and subsequent mar- ket reactions. When using only aggregated senti- ment categories (Model 1), none of the coefficients reach statistical significance, suggesting that simple polarity labels (positive/neutral/negative) alone are insufficient to explain abnormal returns (Table 6). However, once we incorporate the normalized sen- timent scores (Score-1/Score-2) in Model 2, both negative and neutral sentiment become statistically significant (p < 0.05). Interestingly, negative sen- timent is associated with higher returns, while neu- tral sentiment corresponds to lower returns. This suggests that the market interprets weakly framed, cautious, or "neutral-sounding" statements more negatively than explicit negative disclosures poten- tially because neutral framing often masks unfavor- able realities in obfuscated financial language. To further examine where sentiment matters, Models 3 and 4 separate sentiment by document section (Table 7). Only negative sentiment origi- nating from the MD&A section shows significance across specifications. This highlights the informa- tional importance of management’s own narrative; investors appear to react more strongly to adverse sentiment when it is voiced directly by the com- pany’s executives rather than in other sections like Risk or Sustainability. Does aspect-based sentiment from financial re- port affect the stock prices upon release? The results suggest that only certain aspects have significant implications for the market (Table 10). We found that only negative sentiment from the Profit/Loss aspect is statistically significant throughout all window sizes. The coefficients of the model predictors corresponding to aspect-based sentiment are relatively low, indicating that the pos- itive/negative sentiment in each aspect has a small impact on market returns. It is possible that the impact on the market from news and sentiments embedded in Form 56-1 in any sections has already been represented in the prices, as investors and the market have anticipated. Our result further suggest that the market rapidly incorporates new financial performance signals at the report’s release. This table highlights the complexity of sentiment analysis in market reactions, as sentiment polarity does not always align with market outcomes. 7 Conclusion Despite the challenges faced by existing research in financial sentiment analysis, such as outdated methods, limited exploration of advanced natural language processing techniques, and a focus on En- glish text over Thai in studies of the Thai stock mar- ket, our study address these issues from data col- lection to model development. We create the first aspect-sentiment financial dataset tailored specif- ically to Thai financial reports. We adopt BERT- based models to predict aspects and sentiment in fi- nancial annual reports from companies in Thailand. Our model outperforms traditional keyword-based models like MaxEnt and even yields better results than narrow-context model like CNN, emphasiz- ing the significance of broader context required to extract indirect sentiment expression. Moreover, our study highlights the significance of financial documents, particularly Form 56-1 or annual reports, in influencing the Thai stock mar- ket. This is because it introduces new information and reduces data asymmetry issues in the stock market. However, the impact on the sentiment and perception of information in the Thai stock market, as revealed by the regression analysis, suggests that a company’s information affects investor sentiment and perceptions of the market’s performance differ- ently based on the aspect. Furthermore, the impact of sentiment on the market from certain aspect may not align with expectations according to financial theory. Our dataset and resources have been re- leased at https://github.com/nlp-chula/ finnlp-sentiment to facilitate continued research in financial NLP for the Thai market. Non-Linear Scoring Model for Translation Quality Evaluation Serge Gladkoff1, Lifeng Han2, Katerina Gasova3 1Logrus Global, 2LUMC & LIACS, Leiden University, 3MQM Council serge.gladkoff@logrusglobal.com, l.han@lumc.nl, katerina.gasova@gmail.com November 18, 2025 Abstract Analytic Translation Quality Evaluation (TQE), based on Multidimensional Quality Metrics (MQM), has traditionally used a linear error-to-penalty scale calibrated to a reference sample size of 1000–2000 words. However, linear extrapolation is known to bias judgment on samples of a different size than the reference, over-penalizing short samples and under-penalizing long ones, resulting in persistent misalignment with expert intuition. Building on the previously introduced Multi-Range framework [LGM+24], this paper presents a calibrated, non-linear scoring model that aims to better reflect how human content consumers perceive translation quality across samples of variable length. This approach presents empirical data from three large-scale enterprise environments and shows that acceptable error counts grow logarithmically—not linearly—with sample size. This premise is supported by psychophysical and cognitive evidence, including the We- ber–Fechner law and Cognitive Load Theory, which explain why the impact of additional errors diminishes perceptually but grows cognitively with scale. We propose a two-parameter model E(x) = a ln �1 + bx  , a, b > 0, that is anchored to a reference tolerance and calibrated from two tolerance points via a one- dimensional root-finding step. The model yields an explicit interval (in closed form) within which the linear approximation stays within ±20% relative error, and it drops into existing evaluation workflows unchanged apart from a dynamic tolerance function. It improves interpretability, fairness, and Inter-Rater Reliability (IRR) across both human and AI-generated translations. By reinforcing and operationalizing a perceptually valid scoring paradigm, this work advances the field toward a more accurate, scalable, and cognitively grounded translation quality evaluation. The proposed model also aims to provide a better scoring model for further AI-based document-level evaluation congruent with human judgment. Implementation in CAT/LQA systems and implications for human and AI-generated text evaluation are discussed. 1 Introduction Analytic Translation Quality Evaluation (TQE) is widely recognized as the gold standard method for assessing translation quality with high precision. It relies on meticulous annotation of linguistic and technical errors using a consistent typology, often derived from the Multidimensional Quality Metrics (MQM) framework [LUB14], with proper training of annotators. Once the annotations are in place, a scoring model is applied to produce a quantifiable quality assessment. 1 arXiv:2511.13467v1 [cs.CL] 17 Nov 2025 In practical terms, most industry scoring models operate under a linear assumption: the number of allowed errors scales proportionally with the word count of the evaluated sample. This model typically normalizes errors per 1000 or 2000 words to compare them against a client-defined threshold, e.g., no more than five minor errors per 1000 words. The normalized error density is then used to make a pass-or-fail decision or compute a quality score. This method works reasonably well for evaluation sample sizes close to the reference size—that is, the standard word count used as a baseline for comparing results (typically 1,000–2,000 words). This method works reasonably well for evaluation sample sizes close to the reference size—that is, the standard word count used as a baseline for comparing results (typically 1,000–2,000 words). However, problems arise when evaluating smaller or larger samples. Clients, practitioners, and researchers have repeatedly reported a mismatch between the linear model and their holistic judgment of translation quality. Waddington’s comparative studies [Wad99, Wad01] show that additive, points-off models alone do not align with holistic judgments; combining analytic and holistic perspectives improves reliability. This suggests that perceived translation quality is not a linear function. Evidence from other domains points in the same direction. In speech and video quality, international standards report top-end ’compression’ in opinion scores and therefore recommend comparison tasks and non-linear mappings (typically logistic) from objective indices to MOS [ITU96, SWH16, WBSS04]. Within translation industry, QA frameworks encode non- linearity explicitly via severity multipliers and critical ’showstopper’ errors—i.e., one serious defect can outweigh many minor ones [LUB14, SAE16]. Large-scale MT evaluations similarly show that expert, context-aware severity judgments yield system rankings that diverge from simple averages, supporting non-additive scoring [FFG+21]. And in usability engineering, a single ’catastrophic’ issue overrides numerous small problems, mirroring stakeholders’ acceptance behavior for translations [Nie94]. Together, these applied literatures reinforce the conclusion that linear points-off schemes understate how overall quality is perceived and acted upon. In points-off situations, the linear rule makes long samples appear better than experts judge them to be by raising the acceptance threshold in direct proportion to length. A recent quote from a large institutional client illustrates this point: ’Once we started using our current methodology in 2020, we still asked the evaluators to indicate the cases where their actual feeling was different from what the score gave them. We very quickly realized that the main issue was that with very short samples the scoring was overly harsh and with very long samples it was too lenient. The reason for this is that when we evaluate holistically, the perception is not congruent with our scoring formula. For example, we might feel that if a translation sample is about one page, a single major mistranslation error is already enough to judge it as failing; in a seven-page sample, however, seven such errors are far more than we would be willing to tolerate. Instead, we would prefer to fail the sample already at three or four major errors. This poses a problem for the linear scoring model which simply prorates the number of errors per page to a total number of pages in the sample.’ Another client confirmed these findings and chose to avoid the issue by only evaluating samples of exactly 1000 words. However, in real-world operations, such precisely consistent evaluation sample sizes are rare. Evaluation samples often vary significantly in length due to the nature of the content, deadlines, or operational constraints. Despite its known practical shortcomings, the assumption of linear error scaling remains entrenched in industry practice—partly due to implicit conventions and the replication of established procedures, and partly because people often subconsciously apply linear extrapolation to numerical judgments, including those about

the nature of the content, deadlines, or operational constraints. Despite its known practical shortcomings, the assumption of linear error scaling remains entrenched in industry practice—partly due to implicit conventions and the replication of established procedures, and partly because people often subconsciously apply linear extrapolation to numerical judgments, including those about error tolerance. Yet when evaluators (and therefore also content users) assess samples without relying on mental calculation, their judgments reliably deviate from linear expectations. 2 This paper presents empirical evidence and theoretical justification for a non-linear scoring model, first proposed in earlier work on Multi-Range TQE [LGM+24]—one that more accurately captures how content users perceive translation quality as a function of sample length. The present study argues that as the evaluated text gets longer, the maximum number of allowable errors grows, but more and more slowly—equivalently, the perceptionally allowed errors per 1,000 words decline as word count increases. We capture this pattern with a logarithmic dependency. Earlier work [LGM+24] introduced a logarithmic scorecard. This paper shows where that curve comes from: tolerance grows sublinearly with length, as demonstrated by expert surveys and by well-known psychophysical and cognitive results (Weber–Fechner; Cognitive Load Theory); we then provide a simple, easily calibrated model for use in current evaluation tools. 2 Background 2.1 Analytic TQE and MQM Analytic Translation Quality Evaluation (TQE) refers to a structured method of assessing transla- tion output by identifying and categorizing errors in reference to the source text and applicable specifications. Unlike holistic methods, which rely on a general impression of quality, analytic TQE requires systematic annotation of specific error types, each classified under predefined categories. The most prominent and widely adopted framework for such structured annotation is the Multidimensional Quality Metrics (MQM) standard [LUB14]. MQM provides a hierarchical error typology that is flexible and extensible, with high-level error types like Accuracy and Linguistic Conventions (formerly called Fluency) and more granular error subtypes such as Mistranslation, Omission, Grammar, and Spelling. Many specialized metrics used across the industry are subsets or derivatives of MQM, often customized to the type of content or the client’s preference. Once the annotation phase is complete, a scoring model is applied to an evaluation sample (a defined word count from the job), converting the annotated errors into a numeric score or a Pass/Fail verdict. The MQM framework is currently the most detailed and accurate approach to analytic translation-quality evaluation in professional practice. Every MQM-based metric has two inseparable parts: (i) an error typology that specifies which error types are annotated (with a severity level such as minor/major/critical), and (ii) a scoring model that maps those annotations to severity-weighted penalty points and a quality score. For comparability across jobs of different lengths, results are expressed against a reference size—typically 1,000–2,000 words. Refinements to either component therefore directly advance the state of the art in translation- quality measurement. 2.2 Linear Scoring Models and Their Limits The dominant approach to scoring in translation quality evaluation is the linear model. Here, the severity-weighted penalty total (APT, Absolute Penalty Total—the sum of points assigned to annotated errors) is scaled to a reference

the state of the art in translation- quality measurement. 2.2 Linear Scoring Models and Their Limits The dominant approach to scoring in translation quality evaluation is the linear model. Here, the severity-weighted penalty total (APT, Absolute Penalty Total—the sum of points assigned to annotated errors) is scaled to a reference sample size (typically 1,000–2,000 words) so that assessments are comparable across jobs of different lengths. For example, a limit of five minor errors one point each per 1,000 words implies 2.5 penalty points in a 500-word sample and 10 in a 2,000-word sample (and if a major error carries a 5× severity multiplier, a single major error consumes the full 5-point allowance for a sample of 1000 words). Although this proportional scaling appears objective, it fails however to reflect how human content users actually perceive quality. Readers are usually stricter with short texts, where even a single error stands out, and more lenient with longer texts [Wad99, Wad01, LUB14, SAE16]; however, 3 this tolerance wanes as the document length grows further and the errors begin to compound. For instance, as noted above, a single major error is often sufficient to fail a one-page sample; in a seven-page sample, however, evaluators would fail it at far fewer than seven major errors—even though a linear rule would imply proportional tolerance. Such intuitive resistance reveals that human perception of quality is fundamentally non-linear. Building on the Multi-Range Framework proposed in [LGM+24], this paper distinguishes three sample size regimes: • micro-range (< 250 words): For very short samples (under 250 words), traditional quality scoring methods are unreliable. As shown in [GSHA22], quality scores for such brief samples exhibit extremely wide confidence intervals—meaning the range of possible true scores is so large that the measurement is imprecise—making individual measurements meaningless for decision-making. This limitation is particularly important for automatic Quality Estimation (QE), especially with the practice of sentence- or segment-level scoring. Recent industry findings confirm that these fine-grained predictions do not align with how humans perceive quality. Bane[Ban25] highlighted the repeated failures of sentence- or segment-level QE in high-volume translation, where automated scores fail to identify all major, and even critical, errors, making the method unreliable. As discussed in [Gla25], attempting to derive meaningful scores from very small samples or isolated sentences or segments simply does not work. Instead, for micro-range samples, Statistical Quality Control (SQC) methods offer a more statistically robust and risk-aware framework for interpreting quality signals, explicitly framing the producer’s and consumer’s risk associated with very limited observations. • meso-range (≈250−3,000 words): While a Raw score can be useful for certain scenarios, the recommended approach for this range is a Linear Calibrated Scoring Model, anchored to a client-defined tolerance in severity-weighted penalty points (APT) for a reference wordcount. • macro-range (> 3,000 words): Human perception diverges from linear scaling calibrated to a reference sample size in the meso-range, so another linear model is needed; a non-linear (logarithmic) tolerance curve of a Non-Linear Calibrated Scoring Model can instead cover both the meso-range and the macro-range without requiring multiple linear approximations. The present study concentrates on the entire span of statistically reliable measurements in both the meso-range and the macro-range and supplies both psychophysical and empirical evidence for adopting a logarithmic scoring model across these ranges. This paper aims to fill that gap by presenting a non-linear scoring model and providing empirical and theoretical support for it, grounded in psychophysics and cognitive-load research. 3 Empirical Evidence of Non-Linearity To investigate how human perception of translation quality varies with sample length, an empirical study was conducted with quality managers from three large enterprise clients. Each of these organizations manages multilingual translation programs with substantial daily volumes and relies on mature, metric-based TQE systems. 3.1 Survey Design The extended calibration questionnaire described in [LGM+24] was reused, asking survey respondents to state acceptable error counts for multiple evaluation sample sizes without performing linear extrapolation. This method again proved effective in eliciting a latent non-linear response curve. A detailed calibration questionnaire was designed to capture Quality Managers’ intuition about acceptable error tolerance—operationalized as the maximum number of severity-weighted penalty points (APT) they would still pass—across a range of evaluation sample sizes. Importantly, specific measures were taken to neutralize the influence of the standard linear model, which respondents are accustomed to using in their daily work. Without intervention, professionals often default to mental linear math—extrapolating tolerances from known thresholds. Respondents were instructed explicitly not to prorate from known thresholds and to answer from professional judgment alone. The questionnaire deliberately focused on minor errors for two key reasons. First, higher-severity errors (major and critical) are too infrequent for reliable statistical analysis. Second, as many studies note, their impact on quality perception is significantly different and more pronounced. This specific focus is practical, as standard industry practice allows the severity of any error to be expressed as an equivalent number of minor errors. While clients used either words or pages, we normalized all responses for comparison by converting them to a common scale based on a standard of 250 words per page. 3.2 Results The most striking finding was a clear non-linear pattern in error tolerance. Freed from the habit of linear extrapolation, respondents indicated that while they would accept more total errors in longer texts, their tolerance grew far more slowly than the sample size. Instead, the tolerance curve rose steeply at first and then gradually flattened. This pattern was consistent across all three clients, despite differences in their baseline quality standards (the specific error thresholds and performance targets they use) and content types. In very short samples, a single error can be jarring and dominate the user’s entire impression of quality. In longer documents, however, the dynamic shifts: while the perceived impact of any one mistake diminishes, the overall experience is instead degraded by the steady accumulation of minor issues, which erodes trust and creates a sense of general sloppiness. This degradation impacts more than just a pleasant "reading experience"; it affects the content’s practical utility, impairing a user’s ability to perform a task, trust instructions, or operate a product correctly. Ultimately, these findings confirm that the linear scoring model does not reflect how humans judge translation quality: acceptability is not a linear function of error count, because the perceived impact of an error depends on how much text has already been processed—early mistakes loom larger, while later ones add less per unit but accumulate as the sample grows. Consistent with Fig. 7 in [LGM+24], our findings show that linear models overestimate acceptable error counts in the macro-range by up to 50%, while a logarithmic model closely tracks expert judgment throughout the 1-20 page span. Based on this consistent pattern, this paper hypothesizes that human tolerance to translation errors grows logarithmically with the sample size. The rest of this paper explores the theoretical underpinnings of this phenomenon and proposes a formal scoring model that better aligns with real-world perceptions. Using the delta method in App. B, we obtain approximate prediction standard errors and plot shaded confidence bands around the fitted curve. 4 Psychophysical and Cognitive Foundations Empirical findings from these client interviews show that perceived translation quality is not a simple linear function of error count or text length. Instead, human judgment follows deep-seated perceptual and cognitive regularities documented since the nineteenth century [Web34, Fec60, Bor50]. This paper draws on two complementary frameworks—classical psychophysics and modern Cognitive Load Theory—to motivate a logarithmic scoring model. 4.1 Weber–Fechner Law and Logarithmic Perception Psychophysics has long recognized that sensation grows non-linearly with stimulus intensity. In his 1834 monograph on weight discrimination, Weber reported that just-noticeable difference (JND) is a constant fraction of the baseline stimulus: “The smallest perceptible increase of weight bears a fixed ratio to the weight already lifted” [Web34, p. 152]. Three decades later, Fechner integrated Weber’s proportionality into a mathematical model of subjective sensation, arguing that “if equal stimulus ratios yield equal sensation increments, then sensation must be the logarithm of stimulus magnitude” [Fec60, vol. 1, p. 55]. This logarithmic relation—now known as the Weber–Fechner law—was the first quantitative statement of a compressive perceptual scale; an authoritative English translation is provided in [Fec66]. Intuition. Applied to translation quality evaluation, the law would predict that the subjective penalty of an additional error is highest when the text is nearly error-free and decreases as errors accumulate. In other words, the first mistranslation in a short paragraph feels much more jarring than the fifteenth typo in a 20-page report. Subsequent psychophysical research refined, but did not overturn, this insight. Stevens showed that many modalities follow a power function S = k In with exponents n < 1 for brightness, loudness, and heaviness [Ste57]. Although n = 0 is not itself logarithmic, the power-law family In is asymptotically log-like: lim n→0 I n −1 n = ln I. Over finite dynamic ranges, exponents in the 0.2–0.4 band produce curves that closely approximate a logarithmic profile. Over typical stimulus ranges, power exponents n

Over finite dynamic ranges, exponents in the 0.2–0.4 band produce curves that closely approximate a logarithmic profile. Over typical stimulus ranges, power exponents n ∈[0.2, 0.4] are empirically indistinguishable from a log on plots like ours, so a logarithmic tolerance is the parsimonious choice here. Comprehensive reviews such as [Ges97] and the signal detection synthesis of [GS66] confirm that compressive (sublinear) mapping is the norm in vision, audition and touch. Hence, long before today’s quality assessment challenges, experimental psychology had already established a robust theoretical framework: Human judgment converts objective intensities into logarithm-like internal scales. Treating translation errors as discrete ’stimuli’ fits squarely within this tradition and motivates the logarithmic tolerance curve adopted in this paper. 9 4.2 Cognitive Load and Accumulated Impact of Errors Whereas psychophysics explains the decrease in sensitivity to additional stimuli, cognitive psychology accounts for how these stimuli collectively strain mental resources. The theory of limited working memory, formalized as Cognitive Load Theory (CLT), provides a parallel foundation for non-linear perception of translation quality. CLT was introduced by Sweller in the late 1980s as a way to explain why instructional design must respect the cognitive limitations of learners [Swe88]. It builds on earlier findings such as Miller’s famous observation that the number of discrete items a person can hold in short-term memory is limited to approximately seven, plus or minus two [Mil56]. As Sweller notes, “Our capacity to process novel information is extremely limited, and when this limit is exceeded, learning and comprehension suffer” [Swe88, p. 257]. In translation quality evaluation, the same principle applies: each identified error acts as a disruption that requires attentional and interpretive resources. One or two errors may be brushed aside, but a buildup of errors, however minor individually, begins to saturate the evaluator’s cognitive capacity. This leads to increased frustration, reduced comprehension, and a degraded overall impression of quality. Importantly, this degradation does not occur linearly. Just as in perceptual scaling, there is a threshold effect: the cumulative weight of repeated small errors eventually causes a sharp drop in processing fluency. Studies in instructional design and reading comprehension (e.g. [Med20]) have documented how disfluencies compound non-linearly and trigger avoidance behaviors or reduced engagement. Cognitive Load Theory also provides a plausible explanation for the empirical finding that users tend to expect stricter quality in longer documents, even when the overall error density remains stable [Wad99, Wad01]. This reflects a protective mechanism: anticipating that accumulated disruptions will erode comprehension, readers subconsciously raise the standard for what they consider acceptable in large-scale content. Together, these cognitive effects mirror and reinforce the non-linear sensitivity modeled by the Weber–Fechner framework. Although psychophysics focuses on the perceptual scaling of individual stimuli, Cognitive Load Theory models the impact of cumulative disruption. Both lead to the same conclusion: the relationship between perceived translation quality and the raw error count (that is, the objective number of penalty points) is fundamentally non-linear. 4.3 Perception and Cognition

Both lead to the same conclusion: the relationship between perceived translation quality and the raw error count (that is, the objective number of penalty points) is fundamentally non-linear. 4.3 Perception and Cognition Converge on Logarithmic Scoring Together, classical psychophysical scaling [Fec60, Ste57] and cognitive load mechanics [Swe88, Mil56] converge in the same functional form: tolerance for errors grows rapidly at first, then slows logarithmically. A calibrated logarithmic curve therefore offers the most parsimonious way to reconcile (i) diminishing marginal impact of individual errors with (ii) the accelerating cognitive cost of cumulative errors. This synthesis underpins the non-linear scoring model proposed in the next section. 5 Proposed Non-Linear Scoring Model This paper adopts the terminology introduced in [LGM+24], distinguishing between three classes of scoring models. • Raw Score: 100 −α APT/EWC, with α a unit factor (e.g., α = 1000 for “per 1,000 words”). This uses the sample’s penalty rate and is not a calibrated/anchored score. 10 • Calibrated Linear: This scoring model maps a client’s acceptance range (pass/fail tolerance) onto a common 0–100 quality scale, making results easy to read and compare across jobs. • Calibrated Non-Linear: A model that replaces the straight-line rule with a logarithmic tolerance curve. Relative to a linear rule anchored at the reference size, the model is more lenient for short samples and stricter for long ones; total allowance still grows with length, but at a slowing rate. Given both the empirical evidence and the theoretical justifications presented, this paper proposes a more nuanced application of scoring models rather than a complete replacement of the linear approach. While the traditional linear model is often considered sufficient for the meso-range (texts up to 3,000 words), our findings indicate this is precisely where its limitations can be most acute. For example, as shown later in this paper, a linear model calibrated for a 1,000-word reference sample loses significant accuracy (over 20%) when applied to a 2,000-word sample. Therefore, we recommend the non-linear, logarithmic model for all cases where evaluation sample sizes are expected to vary by more than 20% from the reference wordcount (i.e., outside the ±20% fidelity interval defined in §5.4). Both the traditional raw model and the calibrated linear model remain viable tools, but their use should be restricted to scenarios where evaluation sample sizes consistently hover very close to the specific word count for which the models were calibrated. 4 This section introduces the mathematical form of the proposed logarithmic model, explains how it can be calibrated, and demonstrates its practical advantages. By introducing a Non-Linear Calibrated scoring model, this paper extends the MQM scoring apparatus itself, enabling it to represent perceptual tolerance that linear models cannot capture. Severity weights (even exponential ones) change how individual errors are combined within a fixed sample; they do not by themselves make the pass/fail tolerance as a function of sample size non-linear. For example, the ATA certification rubric is an analytic, points-off scheme tailored to short, fixed-length exam translations. Its severity scale is steep (many exponential levels), so higher-severity errors count far more than minor ones, but aggregation is still essentially additive and the exam length is fixed; there is no tolerance curve E(x) that varies with x. Thus ATA and SAE J2450 introduce severity-level non-uniformities, not the sample-size non-linearity addressed in this paper. They are effective for their narrow contexts, but they do not provide the general, non-linear tolerance function E(x) needed to keep scores comparable when evaluation size varies widely. As noted above, many institutional clients describe their scoring guidelines in terms that sound linear—roughly “about one serious error per page” as a tolerable upper bound. In practice, however, evaluators do not extend that allowance proportionally. When the sample expands to seven pages, they do not simply treat seven serious errors as acceptable; instead, reviewers report that they would typically fail such a sample already at three or four serious errors. In other words, tolerance tightens as the sample grows: the acceptable error density falls with text length. What matters is not a linear accumulation of defects, but how those defects shape the perceived quality of the translation as a whole. This asymmetry shows why linear extrapolation is misleading: it inflates the acceptable error count in longer samples and diminishes the perceived severity of errors in shorter ones. 5.2 Mathematical Model This paper proposes the following logarithmic function to model the maximum acceptable number of errors E(x) as a function of sample size x, expressed in words: E(x) = a ln(1 + b x), a > 0, b > 0. Building on the Multi-Range Framework proposed in [LGM+24], this paper distinguishes three regimes of evaluation sample sizes based on their statistical and perceptual characteristics. In the micro-range (fewer than 250 words), evaluation outcomes are highly sensitive to single errors and statistical confidence is very low; thus, risk-based Statistical Quality Control (SQC) is most appropriate. For the meso- and macro-ranges, the choice of an appropriate scoring model depends not on the absolute length of any single text, but on the expected range of fluctuation in evaluation sample sizes. Y-axis: error tolerance (penalty points). 6 Practical Implications To the extent that error tolerance is not linear — as suggested by both empirical findings and practitioner reports — the adoption of a logarithmic scoring model can reshape translation quality evaluation practices, quality management processes, and software tooling across the industry. Replacing the linearity assumption allows quality assessment to become more accurate, consistent, and aligned with human perception. Looking ahead, such a model might also serve as a reference framework for emerging AI-based document-level evaluations. Current AI systems often provide holistic but qualitative judgments with uncertain completeness; a calibrated non-linear scoring model could, in principle, offer a quantitative reference point for future systems that integrate or adjust their evaluations against established calibrated 0–100 quality scale (client-specific PT/MSV mapping). 6.1 Operational Guidelines for Quality Managers One immediate benefit of the non-linear model is its ability to inform and standardize quality expectations across variable evaluation sample sizes. Quality managers can use the calibrated log function to define clear error tolerance thresholds for different content types or use cases, reducing ambiguity when evaluating translation outputs that differ in word count. 17 For example, a quality manager might specify: “Our reference wordcount is 2000 words with a tolerance of 7 minor errors. For evaluation sample sizes between 1500 and 3000 words, the standard linear approximation is acceptable. Outside that range, the logarithmic model must be used to adjust expectations accordingly.” This shift allows quality managers and stakeholders to move beyond one-size-fits-all scoring rules and instead adopt quality scores that reflect actual cognitive effort and perceived severity. In the traditional linear model, these tools calculate scores based on a fixed error density relative to a single reference word count. However, with a logarithmic tolerance function, the score calculation must dynamically adjust based on the actual sample size. This means LQA modules and dashboards need to: • Replace static pass/fail thresholds based on a single anchor point with dynamic tolerance functions, E(x), that adjust based on the actual word count (x). • Visualize quality scores against a curved baseline that represents the tolerance function, not a simple flat line. • Provide evaluators with interactive feedback showing how close a sample’s error count is to its unique, size-adjusted pass/fail threshold. This functionality is particularly valuable for machine translation, post-editing, and AI-generated content, as evaluation samples from these sources often vary widely in word count. 20 7.5 Improvement of a Unified Calibrated Quality Scale One major challenge in TQE is ensuring that quality scores remain human-readable, interpretable, and comparable across different types of content, language pairs, and evaluation sample lengths. The linear calibrated model is a significant improvement over using raw scores with very small passing intervals, but even the linear calibrated model can distort comparability when applied to large or small samples. The linear calibrated model is a significant improvement over using raw scores with very small passing intervals, but even the linear calibrated model can distort comparability when applied to large or small samples. With a non-linear calibrated scoring model, it becomes feasible to normalize all evaluations to a unified, client-specific quality scale. Since the logarithmic tolerance accounts for sample-size effects, and calibration maps results to a common 0–100 (PT/MSV) scale, all evaluations land on the same company-wide quality scale—so scores from jobs of different lengths, language pairs and content types are directly comparable. For example, replicating the English–German marketing case from Table 3 in [LGM+24], a 5,000-word translation with 23 minor errors passed the linear model, but was rejected by human reviewers. The logarithmic model set a threshold of 16 errors—correctly matching the expert decision. This normalization also improves the validity of quality measurement results analytics across a portfolio of projects, enabling better tracking of supplier performance, trend analysis, and root-cause investigations. 7.6 Applications Beyond Human Translation While the immediate application of this model is human translation quality evaluation, the underlying principles are equally relevant to assessing AI-generated content. Large language model (LLM) outputs—such as summaries, answers, or document translations—are increasingly being evaluated using scoring methods similar to those applied for human translation quality evaluation. The model based on non-linear error tolerance provides a fairer and more realistic baseline for evaluating content. It avoids the common pitfalls of unduly penalizing shorter segments with one mistake or overlooking the accumulated minor issues in long, highly fluent AI-generated texts. As organizations adopt more automated content generation, the ability to evaluate quality in a human-aligned, perceptually realistic manner becomes essential. The proposed scoring model provides a foundation for doing so. 7.7 Document-Level Evaluation and Future Automation Translation quality never exists in a vacuum: every segment lives within the cohesive fabric of a document. A translation sample is therefore not a roll of toilet paper to be inspected centimeter by centimeter; its quality must be judged in the context of the larger text. The larger the sample relative to the document, the more faithfully that judgment reflects holistic properties such as cohesion, coherence, register, and terminological consistency. Small extracts can still provide a rapid signal, but offer only a limited view of document quality. They cannot capture discourse-level phenomena, and—because error density interacts non-linearly with length—linear metrics break down outside their narrow reference window. The MQM-based Non-Linear Calibrated model solves this by remaining simple and linear in the meso-range yet extending smoothly into the macro-range. As long as the evaluation sample is suffi- ciently large relative to the document, as recommended by the Multi-Range Framework[LGM+24]—it yields scores that are statistically reliable and consistent with the judgment of experts at the docu- ment level. 21 Of course, analytic TQE becomes increasingly expensive at large evaluation sample sizes. No current AI system can yet perform a complete analytic evaluation, but future models may acquire the ability to conduct formal TQE (full analytic MQM evaluation) over long contexts (document-scale samples), reliably capturing local errors (segment-level) and holistic properties (cohesion, coherence, terminology/style consistency, discourse). The logarithmic model proposed here is expressly designed to serve as the computational backbone for such future automation, ensuring that automated scoring remains perceptually valid across the full spectrum of document lengths. 7.8 Summary In practical terms, the transition to a non-linear scoring model means: • Greater alignment between future automated document-level scoring systems and expert human judgment, • Improved fairness and consistency across evaluation samples of different lengths, • More intelligent quality evaluation systems producing evaluations closer to human perception, • Stronger foundations for evaluating both human and AI-generated translation. This model equips both translation professionals and tool developers with a framework that respects the cognitive and perceptual realities of language evaluation, enhancing decision-making at every level of the translation quality pipeline. The proposed non-linear model captures how translation quality is actually perceived by humans- especially when evaluation sample sizes vary. It is simple to implement, easy to calibrate, and theoretically grounded. By adopting non-linear scoring, evaluation systems can better align numeric scores with human judgment, increasing the reliability and fairness of translation quality evaluations, as well as increasing the reliability and fairness of quality evaluations of translations created by humans or AI-generated texts. 8 Limitations and Future Work The following limitations and research directions qualify the benefits summarized in §7.8 and the conclusion. While the findings and proposed non-linear quality evaluation model presented in this paper are supported by both empirical observation and theoretical grounding, there are important limitations that must be acknowledged. Addressing these will be essential for refining the model and validating its broader applicability. 8.1 Limited Survey Group Size We conducted structured interviews with quality managers at three very large enterprise clients, and the results are corroborated by their internal practices. Despite the scale and maturity of these organizations’ multilingual translation programs, the interview sample is still small. Additional evidence was drawn from our own practice, where we exclusively use a non-linear calibrated scoring model due to its universality and accuracy. However, the tolerance data we used was gathered through expert elicitation and professional experience, rather than under blind experimental conditions—introducing subjectivity and potential sources of bias, including response bias. 22 Further research should involve a broader range of organizations—including LSPs, in-house localization teams, and public-sector translation departments—across different domains and lan- guage pairs. Ideally, future studies should also include controlled experiments where evaluators independently assess translation quality using both holistic judgment and formal scoring models, enabling direct comparison between model predictions and actual pass/fail outcomes. 8.2 Content-Type Specific Effects Different content types (e.g., marketing, legal, technical, UI strings) may have different quality expectations and error tolerance. Tolerance growth is assumed to follow the same logarithmic form

Tolerance growth is assumed to follow the same logarithmic form E(x) = a ln(1 + bx); the two coefficients—a (overall scale) and b (curvature)—may differ by client or use case. We found that a single logarithmic formula performs well across a wide range of content types, suggesting that the logarithmic rule is quite universal—even with fixed parameters. However, this observation requires further validation through broader field data. A valuable extension of this work would be to investigate whether different genres (content types) exhibit distinct curve shapes—for example, steeper or flatter logarithmic profiles—or whether certain domains deviate significantly from the general trend. Such an analysis would help determine whether the proposed model serves as a general framework, as our experience suggests, or represents just one of several viable scoring paradigms. We hypothesize a soft saturation at very large evaluation wordcount due to document-level coherence expectations; future work can test whether E(x) bends further (e.g., log-log or logistic) at book/manual length. 8.3 Severity Weighting and Mixed Error Types This paper concentrates on modeling tolerance in terms of penalty points, each of which typically represents one minor error. In practice, quality evaluations combine several error severities (minor, major, critical) penalized by specific multipliers and sometimes further scaled by different error-type weights applied for different content types. Severity scaling (i.e., fixed severity weights such as minor/major/critical multipliers) is incor- porated by assigning a major or critical error a fixed multiple of the minor penalty points. This is separate from any error-type weights (e.g., terminology vs. grammar) a metric may also define. While a logarithmic curve fits minor-error tolerance well—minor errors being the most frequent and thus the most statistically stable—it may be less suitable for major errors, which occur far less often. For these rarer severities, an integer-valued sequence may be preferable, as indicated by Client 3’s data in Fig. 3. That sequence follows a loosely logarithmic trend but would require explicit rounding rules. Future work should examine the form of such integer sequences, quantify how far they depart from a pure logarithmic curve, and determine the parameters that best describe severity scaling across different content types and languages. 8.4 Inter-Rater Reliability, IRR When a linear model is used, the variability among human raters can be partly attributed to the fact that the model is only accurate at its anchoring point and loses precision elsewhere. In contrast, a calibrated non-linear model better reflects human judgment across a wide range of evaluation sample sizes. As a result, Inter-Rater Reliability (IRR) should increase significantly when using a non-linear calibrated scoring model, as it provides consistent and comparable measurements across 23 different evaluation sample sizes, languages, and content types. More research is needed to quantify the improvement in inter-annotator agreement and to determine how much such a model reduces variance compared to traditional linear approaches in real-world annotation settings.

However, this claim has yet to be formally validated. AI benchmarks which rely on reference-based scoring or raw error density metrics can be improved by introducing calibrated non-linear models which could improve their alignment with human preferences. Future work should involve testing the non-linear model as a normalization layer in LLM evaluation tasks, particularly those involving paragraph- or document-level generation, where holistic perception plays a major role. A further implication is that a calibrated non-linear scoring model could eventually serve as a reference framework for future AI-based document-level evaluations, which currently provide holistic but qualitative judgments without a quantitative calibration. 9 Conclusion Translation quality evaluation plays a critical role in ensuring that multilingual content meets the linguistic, technical, and functional standards required for global communication. While current industry practices predominantly rely on linear scoring models—extrapolating error thresholds proportionally from fixed reference wordcounts—this paper builds on empirical and practitioner evidence showing that linear models do not consistently align with human evaluation, motivating the adoption of non-linear alternatives. This paper presents empirical data from experienced quality managers at large translation buyers, all of whom consistently demonstrated that their internal sense of acceptable error count rises non-linearly with sample size. This effect was evident across organizations, content types, and error categories and severities. This paper further supports these observations with theoretical underpinnings from psychophysics (via the Weber–Fechner law) and cognitive science (via Cognitive Load Theory), both of which explain why perceived quality and impact of errors do not scale linearly with text length. To address this disconnect between the existing scoring systems and human judgment, this paper proposes a calibrated logarithmic scoring model that reflects the genuine growth of error tolerance. This model is mathematically simple, empirically grounded, and easily adaptable to specific client requirements. It provides a flexible, yet rigorous alternative to traditional linear error density calculations. Because it retains a simple two-parameter form—and requires only a one-dimensional solve for calibration—the model is straightforward to integrate into CAT tools, dashboards, and analytics, while providing a unified way to reflect how perceived impact scales with error accumulation. The implications of adopting this model are wide-ranging. Quality managers can gain a more accurate tool for defining passing thresholds in jobs of variable lengths. CAT tools and LQA systems and tools can offer context-aware scoring and fairer quality metrics. Evaluators benefit from consistency that reflects actual perception, and the same principles can be extended to evaluating AI-generated language output. 24 While further research is needed to validate and refine this model, particularly across languages, domains, content types, the fundamental insight seems to be clear:

By embracing this fact, the translation industry can take a critical step toward a more accurate, fair, and human-perception-aligned quality evaluation. Finally, this paper reiterates the warning from [LGM+24]: below the sample size of approximately 250 words, no deterministic tolerance curve is statistically reliable. In such micro-range cases, binomial risk-based Statistical Quality Control (SQC) remains the only viable method.7 This study consolidates the multi-range proposal of [LGM+24] by demonstrating that the same non-linear curve can be independently derived from psychophysical theory and empirical data, thus closing the theoretical gap identified in that earlier work. Exploring Multi-Table Retrieval Through Iterative Search Allaa Boutaleb, Bernd Amann, Rafael Angarita and Hubert Naacke Sorbonne Université, CNRS, LIP6, F-75005 Paris, France {firstname.lastname}@lip6.fr Abstract Open-domain question answering over datalakes requires retrieving and composing information from multiple tables, a challenging subtask that demands semantic relevance and structural coherence (e.g., joinability). While exact optimization methods like Mixed-Integer Programming (MIP) can ensure coherence, their com- putational complexity is often prohibitive. Conversely, simpler greedy heuristics that optimize for query coverage alone often fail to find these coherent, joinable sets. This paper frames multi-table retrieval as an iterative search process, arguing this approach offers advantages in scalability, interpretability, and flexibility. We propose a general framework and a concrete instantiation: a fast, effective Greedy Join-Aware Retrieval algorithm that holistically balances relevance, coverage, and joinability. Experiments across 5 NL2SQL benchmarks demonstrate that our itera- tive method achieves competitive retrieval performance compared to the MIP-based approach while being 4-400x faster depending on the benchmark and search space settings. This work highlights the potential of iterative heuristics for practical, scalable, and composition-aware retrieval. 1 Introduction Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly leverage Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines for natural language interfaces to structured databases [Li et al., 2023, Wang et al., 2024]. In this paradigm, the accuracy and coherence of an LLM’s answer is critically dependent on the retrieval phase: if the retrieved tables do not collectively contain the necessary information or cannot be coherently composed (e.g., via joins), the LLM’s ability to generate a correct answer is severely compromised. While previous work on table retrieval has primarily focused on retrieving individual tables from large corpora [Herzig et al., 2021], complex real-world queries often require retrieving and composing information from multiple tables—a challenge known as multi-table retrieval. This task introduces significant challenges beyond simple relevance ranking. Consider a query like: "Show names and total order values for New York customers who ordered ’Laptop’ and any customers who ordered ’Smartphone’ after 2024." Answering this requires tables like Customers, Orders, and Products, but the retrieval process faces several issues. Due to data redundancy or different valid reasoning paths, multiple valid sets of tables might answer the query. Furthermore, path dependency can arise in iterative methods, where the order of table selection influences the final set. This inherent ambiguity suggests that multi-table retrieval is not always about finding a single, pre-defined optimal set, but often involves exploring multiple plausible evidence paths. Traditional retrieval methods, which assess tables independently, struggle with structural compos- ability. Chen et al. [2024b] addressed this by proposing composition-aware retrieval focused on joinability, reframing the task as selecting a coherent sub-graph. Their Join-Aware Retrieval (JAR) method performs neural retrieval followed by a Mixed-Integer Program (MIP) to find the provably optimal joinable subset. Although highly effective, this one-shot NP-hard optimization suffers in terms of scalability, as acknowledged by the authors. JAR has inspired follow-ups com- Workshop: AI for Tabular Data workshop at EurIPS 2025. arXiv:2511.13418v1 [cs.IR] 17 Nov 2025 bining solver logic with LLMs [Chen et al., 2025] and agentic, multi-hop reasoning approaches like MURRE [Zhang et al., 2025]. Other related works like CRUSH4SQL

scalability, as acknowledged by the authors. JAR has inspired follow-ups com- Workshop: AI for Tabular Data workshop at EurIPS 2025. arXiv:2511.13418v1 [cs.IR] 17 Nov 2025 bining solver logic with LLMs [Chen et al., 2025] and agentic, multi-hop reasoning approaches like MURRE [Zhang et al., 2025]. Other related works like CRUSH4SQL [Kothyari et al., 2023] use a greedy decomposition strategy, but lack the explicit join-aware component central to JAR. Recent works such as DBCopilot [Wang et al., 2025] also explore iterative retrieval via schema routing for massive databases. Complementary to these efforts, recent work has also proposed retrieval-augmented methods that enable LLMs to interact with structured data via iterative and adaptive search frameworks [Wang et al., 2024]. This paper proposes framing multi-table retrieval as an iterative and explorative search process. To stimulate discussion on practical, scalable architectures for this complex retrieval task, we posit that constructing the table set step-by-step offers benefits in scalability (via heuristics), interpretability, and flexibility. Our contributions are threefold: (1) We propose a general, flexible iterative framework for multi-table retrieval. (2) We detail a fast and effective Greedy Join-Aware Retrieval algorithm as a concrete instantiation of this framework. (3) We demonstrate its empirical viability on standard benchmarks (Yu et al. [2018], Li et al. [2023]) as well as more complex enterprise benchmarks (Sen et al. [2020], Chen et al. [2024a]), showing it achieves competitive performance to the MIP-based JAR approach while being over 4-400x faster1. 2 An Iterative Framework for Multi-Table Search We propose framing multi-table retrieval as a sequential decision-making process where an algorithm iteratively expands a set of selected tables based on a dynamic context. This approach offers several advantages over one-shot global optimization: • Interpretability: Each selection step provides a checkpoint for analyzing the reasoning process, potentially enabling human-in-the-loop guidance. • Extensibility: The framework is modular and the selection logic can be dynamically adapted to prioritize different operators (e.g., JOIN vs. UNION) or evolving objectives. • Heuristic Potential: While global optimization is often NP-hard for this task, step-by-step construction lends itself to efficient polynomial-time heuristics, addressing scalability. Representing Query Coverage A central challenge in multi-table retrieval is tracking the capacity to answer the initial query by the already selected tables. To illustrate, consider the query "For movies with the keyword of ’civil war’, calculate the average revenue generated by these movies". To estimate what information is needed, methods process this query using an LLM in different ways. For instance, Kothyari et al. [2023] use the LLM to "hallucinate" a minimal, potential schema (e.g., movies(title, revenue)) that could answer it. In contrast, our method (following Chen et al. [2024b]) decomposes the query into a set of fine-grained concepts or sub-queries {qj}, such as {movies:keyword, movies:revenue}. This general idea of estimating the query’s requirements is known as query coverage. In our framework, query coverage tracks how well each concept qj is addressed by the tables selected so far. coverage. In our framework, query coverage tracks how well each concept qj is addressed by the tables selected so far. Abstract Formulation Let T be the set of all available candidate tables. The search process evolves at each step k a context Ck = (Gk, Qk) where: • Gk = (Sk, Ek) is a graph of k selected tables Sk ⊆T and their discovered relationships Ek (e.g., potential joins). • Qk represents the query coverage state for the query concepts {qj}. For example, in a simple setting we can represent Qk by a vector qk whose size equals the number of concepts, where element qk,j quantifies coverage for concept qj. The process starts with the empty context C0 = ((∅, ∅), 0) with no selected tables and no cov- erage. At each step k, a selection function Φ chooses the next table Tk+1 from the remaining candidates T \ Sk by maximizing a context-dependent utility function U: Tk+1 = Φ(Ck, T \ Sk) = arg maxTi∈T \Sk U(Ti, Ck). An update function Ψ then transitions the system to the next state Ck+1 by incorporating Tk+1: Ck+1 = Ψ(Ck, Tk+1) = (Gk+1, Qk+1). This process repeats until a stopping criterion is met (e.g., k = K or minj qk,j ≥θ). We illustrate a concrete instantiation of the selection and update functions in the next section. 1Code available at: https://github.com/Allaa-boutaleb/iterative-jar/ 2 3 Case Study: Greedy Join-Aware Retrieval In this section we present a simple instantiation of the iterative framework focused on join-aware multi-table retrieval. Our algorithm, like JAR [Chen et al., 2024b], operates on pre-computed scores quantifying relevance and compatibility for a query Q and candidate tables T . These include: • Coarse-grained Relevance (ri), the overall Q-to-table Ti semantic similarity via dense retriever embeddings [Izacard et al., 2022], where emb(·) is the embedding function: ri = cos(emb(Q), emb(Ti)) ∈[−1, 1] (1) • Fine-grained Relevance (Fji), which measures how well Ti addresses a specific sub-query qj (decomposed from Q via an LLM) by finding the maximum similarity between qj and any column c in Ti: Fji = maxc∈cols(Ti) cos(emb(qj), emb(c)) ∈[−1, 1]. • Join Compatibility (ωil), a score in [0, 1] quantifying the join likelihood between Ti and Tl by combining schema, value overlap, and uniqueness signals to approximate a PK-FK link, following Chen et al. [2024b]. The context is Ck = (Gk, Qk) where Gk = (Sk, Ek) is the graph of selected tables Sk and their join paths Ek. The coverage state Qk is implemented as the vector qk storing the maximum Fji score seen for each sub-query qj. The algorithm’s selection function Φ works by maximizing a utility function U that is a weighted sum of three marginal gain components. These gains are calculated for a candidate table Ti relative to the prior context Ck−1 = (Gk−1, Qk−1): • Coarse Relevance Gain, Gcoarse(Ti) = ri, which is intrinsic to the table; • Marginal Coverage Gain, which depends on the prior coverage vector qk−1: Gcov(Ti|Ck−1) = X j max(0, Fji −(qk−1)j) (2) • Marginal Join Gain, Gjoin(Ti|Ck−1) = P Tl∈Sk−1 ωil, which

the prior context Ck−1 = (Gk−1, Qk−1): • Coarse Relevance Gain, Gcoarse(Ti) = ri, which is intrinsic to the table; • Marginal Coverage Gain, which depends on the prior coverage vector qk−1: Gcov(Ti|Ck−1) = X j max(0, Fji −(qk−1)j) (2) • Marginal Join Gain, Gjoin(Ti|Ck−1) = P Tl∈Sk−1 ωil, which depends on the nodes Sk−1 of the prior graph Gk−1. For the main iterative step (k > 1), the utility function U(Ti, Ck−1) combines these gains: Tk = arg max Ti∈T \Sk−1 [λcoarseGcoarse(Ti) + λcovGcov(Ti|Ck−1) + λjoinGjoin(Ti|Ck−1)] (3) The seed selection (k = 1) is a special case. Starting from C0 = ((∅, ∅), 0), the Gjoin term is undefined and Gcov simplifies (as q0 = 0), so the utility function reduces to selecting based on individual merit: T1 = arg max Ti∈T  λcoarse · ri + λcov · X j Fji   (4) Finally, the update function Ψ transitions the state to Ck by updating the graph Gk = (Sk−1 ∪ {Tk}, Ek−1 ∪Enew) and the coverage vector qk = max(qk−1, Fk), where Fk is the vector of fine-grained scores for Tk. 4 Experiments and Analysis Experimental Setup. We compare our iterative greedy algorithm against three baselines: a Dense Retrieval (Contriever) baseline [Izacard et al., 2022], the official JARMIP implementation2 [Chen et al., 2024b], and CRUSH [Kothyari et al., 2023] (using Contriever as the embedding model). For all methods, we use a consistent table schema serialization. The Contriever baseline embeds this serialized schema, the query, and its concepts within the same embedding space to retrieve an initial ranked list of tables. For JAR (MIP) and our iterative method, we re-rank this initial candidate set: the top-20 tables for SPIDER, BIRD, and BEAVER, and the top-30 for FIBEN. Both methods use the identical set of pre-computed relevance (ri, Fji) and join compatibility (ωil) scores, ensuring a fair comparison of the selection algorithms. As shown in Table 1, our greedy method achieves highly competitive, and often superior, retrieval performance compared to the JARMIP baseline, while being dramatically faster. For example, on BIRD at K=3, our method achieves 99% of JAR’s CR score in only 0.7% of the time (101s vs 13679s, a >135x speedup). This efficiency advantage becomes an enabling factor on the complex BEAVER benchmarks. Our iterative method was able to complete all BEAVER-DW runs, while JAR (MIP) timed out on K≥5. On BEAVER-NW (K=5), our method was >240x faster (30s vs 7297s) while achieving a +10.5 point higher CR. It is also worth noting that even when JAR (MIP) finds a 100% optimal solution according to its objective function (e.g., on SPIDER at K=2, see Appendix B), our iterative method can still achieve slightly higher performance (see Table 7). This suggests the MIP’s objective is not a perfect proxy for the end retrieval metrics, further motivating the exploration of alternative heuristic formulations. CRUSH’s lower performance stems from two core design differences: it is not explicitly join-aware, and it employs an aggressive coverage-first greedy logic, unlike our holistic gain-based approach. As analyzed in Appendix D, this heuristic is sensitive to noise and can fail to select optimal tables. Given the performance drop on SPIDER and BIRD, we skipped evaluating CRUSH on FIBEN and BEAVER benchmarks. Finally, the slight performance drop of our method on SPIDER at K=5 and K=10 (relative to the Contriever baseline) can be attributed to the fixed candidate set. As K increases, the re-ranker is 4 forced to include lower-ranked tables from the initial top-20 set, which are more likely to be irrelevant and can create confusion for the selection algorithm on certain queries. 5 Limitations and Future Work This paper proposed reframing multi-table retrieval as an iterative, explorative search process, an alternative to one-shot optimization with inherent advantages in scalability, interpretability, and extensibility. Our Greedy Iterative Join-Aware Multi-Table Retrieval algorithm demonstrated this viability, achieving strong empirical results on standard and complex enterprise benchmarks at a fraction of the computational cost of the MIP-based JAR method [Chen et al., 2024b].While effective, our greedy approach is sensitive to its initial seed selection; a poor start can lead to a suboptimal final set. A crucial direction for future work is to enhance the robustness of the iterative search. The frame- work’s step-by-step nature lends itself well to incorporating backtracking mechanisms. Exploring strategies where the algorithm can revisit earlier decisions if subsequent steps yield low utility could significantly mitigate the risks associated with greedy choices.Furthermore, the framework’s true potential lies in its extensibility beyond joins, such as incorporating the UNION operator. This involves modifying the selection utility U(Ti, Ck) to reward schema compatibility and row diversity. The iterative context Ck allows for dynamic strategies, like prioritizing joins then exploring unions. Exploring such adaptive strategies, potentially learning operator priority, is a rich research avenue. Decision 1: The highest score overall is 0.6121. The table network_1.friend is selected, and segment S2 (high_schooler.student_id) is marked as "covered". • Iteration 2: Selecting the Second Table The algorithm now seeks to cover one of the 3 remaining segments (S1, S3, S4). It ignores segment S2 and any table already selected (network_1.friend). It compares the best scores from unselected tables on uncovered segments: – For network_1.highschooler (Gold): Its best remaining score is 0.5490 (on S3). – For network_2.personfriend (Wrong): Its best remaining score is 0.5597 (on S4). Decision 2: Because 0.5597 > 0.5490, CRUSH greedily selects the incorrect table network_2.personfriend to cover segment S4. Conclusion The baseline’s #2 table, network_1.highschooler, was dropped. Its highest rele- vance score (0.5861 on S2) was "used up" by the first table selected, which had an even higher score (0.6121) on that same segment. CRUSH’s logic then forced it to pick network_2.personfriend because its score on an uncovered segment was marginally higher than network_1.highschooler’s. This case study exemplifies the risk of a purely coverage-based heuristic, which, as noted in Section 4, can be sensitive to noise and lacks the robust, holistic scoring of our iterative, join-aware approach. Attention Grounded Enhancement for Visual Document Retrieval Wanqing Cui cuiwanqing.cwq@taobao.com Alibaba Group Beijing, China Wei Huang huangwei21@mails.ucas.ac.cn University of Chinese Academy of Sciences Beijing, China Yazhi Guo guoyazhi.gyz@taobao.com Alibaba Group Beijing, China Yibo Hu boxuan.hyb@taobao.com Alibaba Group Beijing, China Meiguang Jin meiguang.jmg@taobao.com Alibaba Group Beijing, China Junfeng Ma jack.majf@taobao.com Alibaba Group Beijing, China Keping Bi bikeping@gmail.com University of Chinese Academy of Sciences Beijing, China Abstract Visual document retrieval requires understanding heterogeneous and multi-modal content to satisfy information needs. Recent ad- vances use screenshot-based document encoding with fine-grained late interaction, significantly improving retrieval performance. How- ever, retrievers are still trained with coarse global relevance labels, without revealing which regions support the match. As a result, retrievers tend to rely on surface-level cues and struggle to capture implicit semantic connections, hindering their ability to handle non-extractive queries. To alleviate this problem, we propose a Attention-Grounded REtriever Enhancement (AGREE) framework. AGREE leverages cross-modal attention from multimodal large language models as proxy local supervision to guide the identi- fication of relevant document regions. During training, AGREE combines local signals with the global signals to jointly optimize the retriever, enabling it to learn not only whether documents match, but also which content drives relevance. Experiments on the challenging ViDoRe V2 benchmark show that AGREE signifi- cantly outperforms the global-supervision-only baseline. Quanti- tative and qualitative analyses further demonstrate that AGREE promotes deeper alignment between query terms and document regions, moving beyond surface-level matching toward more ac- curate and interpretable retrieval.
